summary: Describes loop-free alternates, a way to give routers local protection for unicast traffic in IP and MPLS/LDP networks when a link, node, or shared risk link group fails. A router precomputes a backup next hop that will not send traffic back, so it can switch immediately and cut packet loss while the network reconverges.

eli5.summary: A driver who knows a backup route before leaving can turn the instant a road closes. This lets routers prepare a safe backup path ahead of time, so traffic hardly stops when something breaks.

questions: how routers recover quickly from link failure
how do routers avoid micro-loops after a link failure
subtitle: Routers precompute a safe backup next hop, so traffic can switch away from a failed link in tens of milliseconds.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails, link-state routing takes hundreds of milliseconds to converge, and traffic for the affected prefixes is discarded in the meantime. Voice and pseudowire traffic can be sensitive to losses of more than tens of milliseconds.
tldr.mechanism: Each router uses extra shortest-path calculations from its neighbors' viewpoint to find loop-free alternates (LFAs): neighbors whose own shortest path to the destination does not come back through the router. The backup is installed ahead of time and used the moment the primary fails.
tldr.outcome: Routers can repair locally with no support from other routers, but coverage depends on topology. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated by RFC 8518.

today: RFC 5286 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8518. Its basic loop-free alternate rules remain the starting point for this approach to IP Fast Reroute.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
A router's convergence time is generally on the order of hundreds of milliseconds, but interactive services such as VoIP and pseudowires can be sensitive to losses greater than tens of milliseconds. Normally, a router whose local link fails must tell its neighbors through the IGP, recompute new primary next-hops, and only then install them. Until then, traffic for the affected prefixes is discarded.

IP Fast Reroute (IPFRR) aims to cut the reaction time to tens of milliseconds by precomputing an alternate next-hop for each destination. When the link to the primary next-hop fails, the router switches to the alternate until it has run a new SPF and installed the results. Computing the alternate does not alter the primary computed by the standard SPF.

The mechanism assumes a link-state IGP (OSPF or IS-IS, for IPv4 or IPv6), and that both the primary and alternate paths are in the same routing area. It covers intra-domain routing only. Fast reroute for BGP inter-domain routing is not part of it.
sections.eli5: When a road closes, cars normally stop until the map app finds a new route. Here, each router writes down a spare route in advance and uses it right away.

sections.title: Failure Scenarios and Micro-Loops
sections.content:
An alternate may protect against a single link failure, a single node failure, a shared risk link group (SRLG), or a combination. If a failure is bigger than the alternate was designed for, traffic can briefly loop until the next full SPF. For example, if a link-protecting alternate is used and the neighbor router itself fails, both the router and its alternate neighbor may switch to their alternates and send the traffic back and forth.

Two ways avoid this. A node-protecting LFA protects against loss of the neighbor. A downstream path is an alternate whose neighbor is strictly closer to the destination than the calculating router, so each router on the path is closer than the one before and no micro-loop can form. The cost is coverage: downstream paths alone can severely limit it. A router SHOULD select a link-and-node-protecting LFA over a link-protecting downstream path.

For correlated failures, general SRLGs could add unacceptable computational complexity, so the RFC handles a subset called local-SRLGs, where all member links have one end on the same router (for example VLANs on one Ethernet interface, or links on one line card).
sections.eli5: If your backup road goes through the very town that just lost power, you can end up driving in circles. So the router checks that its backup does not lead back to it, and prefers backups that also survive a whole-neighbor failure.

sections.title: Computing Loop-Free Alternates
sections.content:
Let S be the calculating router, N a neighbor, and D the destination, with Distance_opt(X,Y) the shortest distance from X to Y. A neighbor N is a loop-free alternate if and only if Distance_opt(N, D) < Distance_opt(N, S) + Distance_opt(S, D). Implementations MUST meet at least this condition. In words: N's best path to D must not pass through S.

To evaluate this, S needs its own distance to D (from the regular SPF) plus the distances from each neighbor to D and to S. These come from extra SPF runs rooted at each neighbor.

For node protection against primary neighbor E, N must also satisfy Distance_opt(N, D) < Distance_opt(N, E) + Distance_opt(E, D). If the two sides are merely equal, the alternate SHOULD be assumed not to give node protection, because N's equal-cost path might go through E.

On broadcast and NBMA links, the link is modelled as a pseudo-node, and a link-protecting alternate SHOULD be loop-free with respect to that pseudo-node. Also, S must pick a next-hop toward N that avoids the pseudo-node.

With ECMP, alternates are computed for each primary next-hop separately; another primary next-hop can serve as an alternate but is not guaranteed to protect against the failure.

A router MUST NOT use an alternate along a link whose cost or reverse cost is LSInfinity (OSPF) or maximum cost (IS-IS), or which has the IS-IS overload bit set, so that routers following RFC 3137 and links costed out for maintenance stay free of traffic.
sections.eli5: A neighbor is a safe backup only if its own shortest way to the destination does not go through you. Otherwise it would hand the traffic straight back.

sections.title: Choosing Among Alternates
sections.content:
A router SHOULD try to select at least one LFA for each primary next-hop, though it MAY decide not to use one that does not protect the failure scenario of interest. The selection rules are:

  • Prefer a loop-free node-protecting alternate; otherwise MAY use a link-protecting one.
  • Prefer a link-and-node-protecting alternate over a node-protecting one that is not link-protecting.
  • With several primary next-hops, prefer one of the other primaries or a node-protecting LFA.
  • Implementations SHOULD support a mode that prefers other ECMP primaries over any non-primary alternate, to keep regular ECMP traffic patterns.
  • Implementations considering SRLGs MAY use SRLG protection to rule alternates out.

The RFC includes a step-by-step algorithm, given for information only; any algorithm that satisfies the rules is acceptable. Section 3.7 lays out the trade-offs, and section 3.8 describes a simplification that computes only one link-protecting LFA per next-hop, at the price of reduced coverage.
sections.eli5: If a router has several spare roads, it picks the one that stays safe in the most kinds of trouble, and it likes spare roads that it already uses anyway.

sections.title: Using and Dropping an Alternate
sections.content:
When a next-hop failure is detected, the router SHOULD remove the failed primary and install the LFA computed for it, if it is not already installed. The alternate MUST be used only for traffic routed along shortest paths. Multicast is out of scope.

A router MUST limit how long it keeps using the alternate after the primary becomes unavailable, so it moves to the new primaries once the network has converged. The RFC explains why it can be wise to hold on a little longer: if S switched to its new primary immediately, that neighbor might not yet have updated, and the traffic could loop and be dropped. Because the alternate's path is known not to go via S or the failed element, delaying the new primaries is safe while the single-failure assumption holds.

Use of the alternate SHOULD end when the new primary was loop-free before the topology change, when a configured hold-down expires, or when notice of an unrelated topology change arrives.

For LDP, a router must distribute labels to all neighbors (not only upstream ones), use liberal label retention, and should use downstream unsolicited mode, so labels for the alternate are ready before the failure. No targeted sessions or signaling extensions are then needed.
sections.eli5: After the crash, the router keeps using the spare road for a little while, until everyone else has caught up with the new map. Switching too early could make cars go in circles.

sections.title: Routing Protocol Aspects
sections.content:
For a multi-homed prefix, announced by several routers, the best protection comes from treating the prefix as a node in the SPF with unidirectional links from each router that advertises it. A router SHOULD compute the alternate by considering all of those routers, and MAY simplify by assuming the prefix is attached only to its pre-failure best attachment point, at the risk of missing a possible repair.

OSPF multi-area networks bring complications, because a path can leave an area and re-enter it. Section 2 therefore says LFAs should not be used in the backbone area when virtual links exist (unless each transit area has a full mesh of virtual links between ABRs), nor in several alternate-ABR and external-route cases listed there. Appendix A gives a worked example involving an ASBR that is also an ABR. When an AS-external LSA carries a forwarding address, alternates SHOULD be computed toward the forwarding address.

BGP simply inherits the IGP alternate to the AS exit router, and the BGP decision process is unchanged. Multicast is out of scope, and alternates SHOULD NOT be used for multicast RPF checks. Multi-topology IS-IS and OSPF are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some places can be reached through more than one door, and some towns have roads that leave a district and come back. In those cases the router has to be extra careful, and sometimes it simply does not use a spare road.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism does not modify any routing protocol messages, so it introduces no new threats from packet modification or replay. Traffic to some destinations may briefly go through next-hop routers that would not be used otherwise, but those routers can be used anyway when a different topology change occurs, so the RFC does not view this as a new threat.

For LDP, labels are distributed more widely, but still only to neighbors with a trusted LDP session. This and the recommendation of liberal label retention are believed to have no significant security impact.
sections.eli5: The router does not change any of the messages routers send each other, so the trick does not give attackers new tools.

data.title: Loop-free tests for neighbor N, router S, destination D
data.code:
Inequality 1 (loop-free):
  D_opt(N, D) < D_opt(N, S) + D_opt(S, D)

Inequality 2 (downstream path):
  D_opt(N, D) < D_opt(S, D)

Inequality 3 (node-protecting, primary neighbor E):
  D_opt(N, D) < D_opt(N, E) + D_opt(E, D)
